title: Sustainable design
examples: How can we make a product last longer?
Can you give an example of 'refusing' something?

explain.say: Today we will explore sustainable design practices for products.

items: Reuse: using something again for its original purpose
Refurbish: restoring something to good condition
Repair: fixing something that is broken
Recycle: processing waste into new materials

explain.say: The first 'R' is reduce, which means using less stuff.
Repurposing means giving an item a completely new job.

draw.text: Repurpose: New function for old item

explain.say: Life-cycle thinking looks at a product from start to finish.
Consider the life cycle of a plastic water bottle.

items: Use | Bottle is filled and used

explain.say: In everyday life, think about an old pair of jeans.

faq.q: What is the difference between reusing and repurposing?
faq.a: Reusing means using something for the same purpose it was made for. Repurposing means changing its function entirely.
asks: Can you give me an example of reusing?
Is repurposing always better than reusing?

faq.q: Does 'reducing' always mean throwing things away?
faq.a: No, reducing means minimizing the amount of resources needed in the first place. It is about prevention.
asks: What is the best way to reduce waste?
Does reducing affect the design stage?

faq.q: Why is looking at the whole life cycle important?
faq.a: It helps us see where waste is created, not just at the end. We can fix problems earlier in the process.
asks: What does 'life-cycle thinking' mean for designers?
Should we only focus on recycling?

faq.q: Is refurbishing the same as repairing?
faq.a: No, repairing fixes a broken part to make it work again. Refurbishing restores the whole item to a high standard, often making it look new.
asks: What is the difference between fixing and restoring?

faq.q: What is the most sustainable option for a new product?
faq.a: The most sustainable option is usually to design it so it can be easily repaired or taken apart for recycling.
asks: Is it better to buy used or new?
Which 'R' is the best one to aim for?

facts: Designing for disassembly makes recycling easier at the end of life.
The 6 Rs include Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Refurbish, Repair, and Recycle.
Life-cycle thinking considers environmental impact from raw material extraction to final disposal.
Reducing consumption is the most effective way to minimize waste.

quiz.say: A company takes old glass bottles and melts them down to make new window panes. Which 'R' is this?
quiz.show: Melting glass bottles into new panes.
quiz.why: Recycling involves processing waste materials into raw materials for new products.

wrong.0: Reuse means using the bottle again without changing it.
wrong.1: Repurposing means giving the bottle a completely new job, like a vase.
wrong.2: Refurbishing means cleaning and restoring the bottle to look brand new.

quiz.say: A student uses old t-shirts to make cleaning cloths instead of buying new ones. What concept is this?
quiz.show: Using old shirts for cleaning cloths.
quiz.why: Repurposing means giving the item a new function, like cleaning cloths.

wrong.0: Repairing means fixing a tear in the t-shirt so it can still be worn.
wrong.1: Reducing means not buying any t-shirts at all.
wrong.3: Reusing would mean wearing the t-shirt again for the same purpose.

quiz.say: A designer plans a phone that uses easily separated, non-toxic materials. This shows consideration for:
quiz.why: Considering how a product ends its life is key to life-cycle thinking.

wrong.0: Marketing appeal only looks at how good it sells.
wrong.2: Initial cost only looks at the price when buying it.
wrong.3: Manufacturing speed only looks at how fast it is built.
